This causes the function to return incorrect historical balances — for example, if a user had 1000 at block 100, then 1500 at block 150, and the system queries for block 120, it returns 1500 instead of 1000. This breaks reward calculations in voting_reward and cabal modules that rely on accurate historical snapshots. The caller expects a true snapshot value at the exact block height, but receives the most recent snapshot <= requested height, creating a representation boundary violation.

extra_findings.title: Desynchronized Supply Snapshot Update in snapshot()
extra_findings.description: The snapshot() function updates supply_snapshots using coin::supply(metadata) at the time of snapshot, but does not ensure that all holder balances have been snapshotted before this update. If a user mints tokens between the time snapshot() is called and when the supply is read, the supply snapshot becomes inconsistent with individual holder snapshots. For example, if the total supply is 10,000 and 5,000 is held by user A, and user B mints 1,000 after snapshot() starts but before coin::supply() is called, the supply snapshot becomes 11,000 while user A's snapshot remains 5,000 — creating a 1,000 discrepancy. This breaks the invariant that sum(holder snapshots) == supply snapshot. The result is that reward distributions based on proportional shares become mathematically invalid, causing under- or over-distribution of rewards to users.

extra_findings.title: Lazy Snapshot Write Can Miss Balances Due to Non-Contiguous Block Gaps
extra_findings.description: The check_snapshot function only writes a snapshot entry if the current block height > snapshot_block and no entry exists for snapshot_block. However, if blocks are skipped (e.g., due to L2 finality delays or reorgs), and a user's balance changes during the gap, the system never records the balance at the intended snapshot block. For example, if snapshot_block = 100, and the next block is 105, and the user's balance changes from 1000 to 1200 between blocks 101-104, check_snapshot will not write a snapshot at block 100 because current_block_height (105) > 100, but it also won't write a snapshot for block 100 because it only writes when the key is missing — and the key for block 100 was never created. Thus, get_snapshot_balance will fall back to current balance (1200) instead of the true snapshot (1000), causing reward miscalculations. This violates the assumption that snapshot entries are written for every snapshot block, leading to data loss.

extra_findings.title: Incorrect Snapshot Balance Fallback in get_snapshot_balance_internal with Empty Table
extra_findings.description: When get_snapshot_balance_internal encounters an empty snapshot table, it returns the current balance (cabal_balance.balance) as the snapshot value. However, this is only valid if the user has never had a prior snapshot. If the user had a snapshot at block 50, then their balance changed, and the snapshot table was cleared (e.g., via bug or malicious action), the function incorrectly returns the current balance as the historical snapshot. This allows an attacker to clear their snapshot table (e.g., via a bug in another module) and then claim a higher historical balance than they ever had. For example, if a user had 1000 at block 50, then 2000 at block 100, and the snapshot table is cleared, get_snapshot_balance(..., 50) returns 2000 instead of 1000 — inflating their reward share by 100%.

extra_findings.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds via Reward Metadata Transfer Triggers Unintended Reward Distribution
extra_findings.description: The contract automatically processes any transfer of reward tokens (vault::reward_metadata()) to the VIP contract address as a signal to distribute rewards, even when the transfer originates from system operations (e.g., bridge deposits or external fund returns). This allows an attacker to trigger reward distribution to arbitrary users by sending reward tokens to the VIP contract, effectively creating a mechanism where system-initiated fund returns are misinterpreted as user-eligible deposits. This leads to unauthorized reward claims and protocol loss.
